lessons.title: Should You Sell, Hold, or Buy the Dip?

body.text: Sell, hold, or buy more. The three choices during a crash are not equally good, but the worst outcome usually comes from making the choice in panic, with no framework at all.

children.text: Lesson 3.2 ended with a question: has your actual reason for investing changed, or has only the price changed? This lesson turns that question into a proper decision framework, covering when each of the three options genuinely makes sense, and the maths behind why continuing to invest through a downturn often works better than most people expect.

Selling during a downturn is the right call in two specific situations, and neither of them is "the market feels scary right now." The first is a genuine, near term need for that exact money, a goal within the next one to three years such as a child's admission fee or a planned medical expense, where you cannot afford to wait out a recovery that might take months or years. The second is when your original reason for owning that investment has actually broken: a company's business has genuinely deteriorated, not just its share price, or an index fund no longer fits your actual goals. Selling purely because prices fell, with neither of these two reasons present, usually means locking in a loss right before the eventual recovery, exactly the pattern seen in both 2008 and 2020.

Holding is the sensible default for money you do not need for several years, invested in something whose fundamentals have not changed. It requires nothing except emotional discipline, which is genuinely hard when a portfolio is down 30% and every news channel is repeating the word crash. It is also, by the evidence of Lesson 3.2, the choice that worked for anyone who stayed invested in a broad Nifty or Sensex index through both 2008 and 2020, all the way to full recovery and beyond.
Option 3: Buy the Dip, the Smart Way

markDefs.definition: Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals regardless of price, which automatically buys more units when prices are low and fewer units when prices are high, lowering your average cost per unit compared to investing the same total amount all at once at a random time.

children.text: "Buy the dip" usually conjures an image of correctly guessing the exact bottom and putting in a lump sum. That is extremely difficult even for professionals, and unnecessary for most investors. The far more reliable version of buying the dip is simply continuing a Systematic Investment Plan, an SIP, through the downturn instead of pausing it, which is a form of
. A fixed monthly amount buys more units automatically when the NAV is low, which is exactly the discount a falling market is offering you, without requiring you to correctly predict anything.

body.context: Total invested ₹40,000 buys 478.97 units, an average cost of about ₹83.5 per unit, lower than the simple average price of ₹85.0 across the four months, because more units were bought in the cheaper months

body.text: Continuing an SIP through a downturn only makes sense with money you will not need for years and genuine conviction in what you are invested in. It is not a reason to invest money earmarked for near term expenses, and it does not protect you from a permanent loss if the underlying investment's fundamentals have actually broken.

body.caption: When each option actually makes sense

cells: You need the money within 1 to 3 years, or the fundamentals genuinely broke
You are reacting only to the price falling and the news being loud
The money is for a goal several years away and the thesis is intact
You cannot emotionally tolerate watching the value stay lower for a while
You have genuine surplus money and years of runway ahead
The extra money is actually needed soon, or your emergency fund is not intact

body.title: Before You Decide
steps: Confirm your emergency fund, roughly 6 months of expenses in something safe and liquid like a fixed deposit or liquid fund, is intact and untouched
Check the actual time horizon for this specific money, not your portfolio in general
Ask whether the underlying business or index's fundamentals have genuinely changed, or only the price has
Notice whether your urge to act is coming from a plan you set earlier, or from today's headlines
If you decide to hold or continue investing, write down why, so you have something other than memory to check yourself against later

body.title: Apply the Framework
body.scenario: The Nifty has fallen 22% over four months. You have a ₹5,000 monthly SIP into a Nifty index fund for a retirement goal 20 years away, and a separate ₹2 lakh fixed deposit maturing next month that you were planning to use for a family wedding in three months.
body.prompt: What would you do with the SIP, and what would you do with the fixed deposit maturity amount, and why are these two decisions different?
body.modelAnswer: The SIP should almost certainly continue. The goal is 20 years away, the fundamentals of a broad index have not broken just because prices fell 22%, and continuing actually buys more units at the lower NAV, working in your favour through rupee cost averaging. The fixed deposit maturity money is a completely different case: it is needed in three months for a wedding, which is a near term, non-negotiable goal. Moving that money into equities now, even at lower prices, would expose money you cannot afford to lose in the short term to further declines, which is exactly the kind of near term need that argues against buying the dip. Same market conditions, two different correct decisions, because the time horizon and purpose of the money are different.

body.title: Test Yourself
body.question: Why does a fixed monthly SIP amount typically produce a lower average cost per unit than a single lump sum invested at a random point in time, when NAV is volatile?
options: SIPs always guarantee higher returns than lump sum investing
A fixed amount automatically buys more units when NAV is low and fewer when it is high, pulling the average cost down
Mutual funds charge lower fees on SIP investments
SIPs are not affected by market crashes at all
body.explanation: Because the rupee amount is fixed each month, a lower NAV buys proportionally more units and a higher NAV buys fewer, which naturally pulls the average cost per unit below the simple average of the prices paid. This is rupee cost averaging, not a guarantee of higher returns, just a disciplined way of buying more when things are cheaper.

body.text: This lesson offers a general decision framework for educational purposes, not personalised financial advice. Your own decision should account for your full financial situation, and a SEBI registered investment adviser can help apply this thinking to your specific circumstances.

points: Sell only for two reasons: you genuinely need the money within one to three years, or the underlying fundamentals have actually broken, not just the price
Hold is the sensible default for long horizon money in an investment whose thesis is still intact
The reliable version of buying the dip is continuing an SIP through a downturn, which uses rupee cost averaging to buy more units automatically at lower prices
In a four month example with NAVs of 100, 80, 70, and 90, a fixed monthly investment produced an average cost of about ₹83.5 per unit, lower than the simple average price of ₹85.0
The same market conditions can call for different decisions depending on the time horizon and purpose of each pool of money, as the SIP versus fixed deposit example shows
Before deciding anything, check your emergency fund, your actual time horizon, and whether you are reacting to a plan or to a headline
